book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell

chapters.file: ch03 - KISS and Philosophy Wiser than Hell.md

chapters.relation: Editor Courtland Lewis's introduction argues that KISS — the make-up, pyrotechnics, anthems, libido-centered songs, and even the 'Knights in Satan's Service' rumor — makes the band irresistible material for philosophy, quoting Gene Simmons's claim that KISS's original philosophy was 'to create magic and to encourage the suspension of disbelief.' It lays out the volume's structure (sections for the Demon, Space Ace, Starchild, Catman, and Fox) and previews each contributor's chapter, from Siler on the Message to Rentmeester on Kondoms and Kaskets. Lewis closes with personal testimony that KISS's message of perseverance kept him from ever giving up.

R. Alan Siler argues that KISS's deepest and most consistent philosophy is a message of self-belief: work hard, believe in yourself, never give up. He traces it from 'Shout It Out Loud''s 'treat yourself like Number 1' and 'Flaming Youth' through The Elder's oath narrative ('only you are the answer') and its closing declaration 'I believe in me,' to Eric Carr's 'Little Caesar' and Carr's final backing vocals on 'God Gave Rock'n'Roll to You II,' reading Carr's scrappy rise and death as the Message incarnate. Siler contends the Eighties albums are the Message's peak and closes by showing how adherence to it organized his own life accomplishments.

chapters.file: ch10 - 2. KISStory and Kulture of the Hottest Band in the World.md
chapters.relation: Historian and lifelong fan Matt Alschbach argues that the history of KISS is the history of its fans: his police-officer father taking him to the 1979 San Diego show, schoolyard debates over Alive! versus Alive II, rubbing pencil shadings over the Double Platinum gatefold to guess the band's faces, and strangers' comments on his KISS T-shirts all show the band forging identity and community. He recounts how Alive! rescued Casablanca Records, how the 1983 MTV unmasking and 1996 remasking reinvented the brand for new generations, and how the KISS KRUISE, $50,000 Vault Experience, and Rock & Brews extend its cultural reach. The chapter's claim is that KISS fandom supplies camaraderie, family bonds, and life-meaning across generations.

chapters.file: ch11 - 3. Paul’s Lick It Up Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Courtland Lewis reads Paul Stanley's autobiographies (Face the Music, Backstage Pass) and songs as a worked-out life philosophy. Stanley's turn from chasing approval to confronting his inner pain exemplifies Socrates' unexamined-life dictum; 'Reason to Live' is glossed through Camus's Sisyphus — ground your reason to live in something indestructible, your own self-chosen meaning — while Plato's Ion explains Stanley's mix of learned craft and divine-inspired performance. Aristotle's flourishing through moderation appears in the advice not to overplay 'Rock and Roll All Nite,' and Lewis adds Locke and Rousseau on how laws, boundaries, and education create rather than restrict freedom, closing with Stanley's 'questioning ourselves is not a weakness' as Socratic wisdom.

Donald Presley debunks the claim that KISS are 'Knights in Satan's Service' by showing the pitchfork Satan is a pop-culture invention — tracing the Adversary from the Book of Job through Zoroastrian influence, Dante, and Milton — and arguing that branding Gene's Demon persona or songs like 'God of Thunder' and 'Unholy' as evil commits the informal fallacy of missing the point. He then argues, ironically, that KISS's actual values — hard work, self-empowerment, sexual freedom, indulgence without harming others — overlap substantially with the real LaVeyan Satanism of The Satanic Bible and with Aristotle's ideal of moderately indulging natural goods (sex, alcohol, success) for the sake of flourishing. The conclusion: KISS is not Satanic, but its life-affirming message coincidentally mirrors Satanism's actual teachings, and Christians, KISS, and Satanic virtues can coexist.

Courtland Lewis uses KISS's career gambles to compare theories of decision-making. After Tolstoy's twig-over-the-dragon allegory of mortal life, he tests W.K. Clifford's shipowner (never act without sufficient evidence) against KISS's counter-evidence bet on the Alive! live album, models the choice with Pascal's Wager, and uses the Prisoner's Dilemma to explain the flop of the four 1978 solo albums. He then argues William James's pragmatism — beliefs as rules for action, the living, forced, and momentous option that 'KISS is the best' — best explains why acting on the band's self-created narrative was authentic, with Nietzsche completing the picture: greatness requires leaping, living dangerously, tightrope-walking toward self-defined success.

Peter Finocchiaro takes Gene Simmons's and manager Doc McGhee's suggestions that KISS could become a franchise — new musicians stepping into the Demon and Starchild roles — and works out what band identity could mean. Using the Ship of Theseus, he distinguishes qualitative from numerical identity, invokes collective intentionality to explain how a band without a mind can perform intentional actions, and contrasts the 'originality connection' (being the actual founding members) with the 'continuity connection' (day-by-day chained succession), mirroring the bodily-versus-psychological debate about Gene Simmons's personal identity. His conclusion is that bands are governed by social rules fans collectively create — like the rules of basketball or musical genre — so in his imaginary two-KISS scenario, and for any future franchise, the fan base would decide which band is the real KISS rather than discovering a pre-existing fact.

L.A. Recoder's densely dialectical essay presents KISS as a 'philosophical toy' that taught him creativity through destruction, pivoting on Paul Stanley's line that 'we loved you until we strapped on our guitars, and then we were there to destroy you.' He reads the oral history of KISS upstaging Black Sabbath — the 'KISS! KISS! KISS!' chant that got them thrown off the tour — and Ted Nugent's challenged escalation as the destroyer's veneration-through-destruction, then reads Chuck Schuldiner's death-metal band Death covering 'God of Thunder' as Hegel's tarrying with the negative: the KISS of Death turns round upon itself to become the Death of KISS, through which KISS is reborn.

Randall Auxier builds a characterology of the four personae using Aristotle's methods (endoxa and aporia) and the band's wealth hierarchy as his map. The Demon is Nietzsche — an uninhibited cosmopolitan beyond good and evil who philosophizes with a hammer and whispers eternal recurrence; the Starchild is Epicurus — Paul's microtia and bullied childhood formed the detached soul that Plato's Republic ties to being a philosopher, yielding ataraxia, aponia, therapy, and disciplined long-term pleasures; the Catman has Kundera's lightness of being around 'Beth'; and the Spaceman's otherworldly detachment explains both his guitar genius and the Nazi-regalia incident. The chapter's thesis: KISS succeeded because Gene and Paul's detached, centered self-knowledge let them give fans exactly what they secretly wanted.

chapters.file: ch18 - 9. KISS the Ship of Theseus Goodbye!.md
chapters.relation: Shane Ralston asks whether KISS, after constant lineup changes that left only Stanley and Simmons fixtures, is still the same band. He lays out Plutarch's Ship of Theseus and Hobbes's harder variant — a ship rebuilt from the salvaged original planks — formalizing three assumptions (endurance through gradual change, identity with parts, transitivity of identity) and their conflicting conclusions, then applies a fifty-percent-plus-quality reading: keeping the two powerhouse founding members preserved KISS's core identity through the Carr, Vincent, St. John, Kulick, Singer, and Thayer eras. For the imagined duplicate-KISS case he deploys Chisholm's 'loose and popular sense' of identity and Ted Sider's four-dimensionalist 'space-time worm,' concluding the dispute is practical — best settled by courts of law, not armchair metaphysics.

chapters.file: ch20 - 10. KISS Was Made for Lovin’ You.md
chapters.relation: Courtland Lewis categorizes virtually the entire KISS catalogue by kind of love. Using Nicholas Wolterstorff's distinctions, he sorts erotic-activity songs ('Uh! All Night,' 'Deuce'), erotic-attachment songs ('I Still Love You,' 'Calling Dr. Love'), and erotic-attraction songs ('I Was Made for Lovin' You,' 'Hotter than Hell'), flags the disturbing near-statutory trio ('Christine Sixteen,' 'Goin' Blind,' 'Domino'), and adds non-erotic attachment, philia ('Childhood's End'), agape ('I Will Be There'), and the thirty-three percent of songs advocating a way of life ('Lick It Up' as an anti-suicide anthem of self-reclamation). He concludes with Aristotle and Plato on flourishing and Wolterstorff's claim that lives are 'shot through with love,' inviting readers to re-sort the lists with better reasons.

Robert Vuckovich reads KISS's sex songs through Aristippus of Cyrene's hedonism: immediate bodily pleasure is the highest good, so the 'urge to merge' of 'Fits Like a Glove,' the whips of 'Sweet Pain,' the persuasion of 'Nothin' to Lose,' and the stewardess encounter of 'Room Service' are candid validations of pleasure — morally acceptable where desire and consent are mutual. Aristippus's cautions (the prostitute visit, the three courtesans he declined, his non-exclusive arrangement with Lais) ground the chapter's limits on excess, mirrored in Gene passing girls to Point Blank's guitarist and Paul's shift to quality over quantity. The Cyrenaic alternation of work and play matches KISS's 'God Gave Rock'n'Roll to You II' ethic — sweat first, then indulge — and Cicero's report that the body is 'nature's canon and rule' closes the case.

chapters.file: ch22 - 12. An Intimate Look at Paul Stanley’s Love.md
chapters.relation: Robert Grant Price maps Paul Stanley's catalogue onto four loves. Eros as soulmate-love follows Aristophanes' split-beings myth from Plato's Symposium ('Forever,' 'Every Time I Look at You'); self-love follows Aquinas's demand that it be 'rightly ordered,' so Stanley's machismo songs pass while Gene's 'I' fails as disordered egomania; bodily love is defended as bawdy dramatic monologue — foreplay between lovers rather than instruction in reducing women to sex objects; and love of life is secularized agape praise in 'I'm Alive,' 'Shout It Out Loud,' and the very title Alive!. Price then asks why love drives art at all, weighing the transcendentals (true, good, beautiful) against the Scruton-versus-Craig-Martin can-of-shit debate, and reads 'Reason to Live' as the claim that only rightly ordered love can ground a life.

chapters.file: ch23 - 13. You Wanted the Best, You’ve Got the Right to the Best.md
chapters.relation: Mikko Puumala invents a 'Preservationist' who argues that future generations have a right to the chance of experiencing a live KISS show, by analogy with preserving the Colosseum and Niagara Falls, and then dismantles the argument. A reductio ad absurdum shows the principle would oblige preserving nearly every rock band; the Castle thought experiment exposes the problem that after the End of the Road tour there is no fact about which historical KISS (masked Seventies, unmasked Eighties, reunion era) should be restored; and the museumization worry shows that freezing KISS would contradict the adaptability — disco, glam, grunge — that defines KISStory. He concludes there is no duty on Simmons and Stanley to keep KISS alive, though a modest utilitarian case favors the show going on.

chapters.file: ch25 - 14. The Joyful Relativity of Kondoms and Kaskets.md
chapters.relation: Casey Rentmeester reads KISS through Nietzsche and Mikhail Bakhtin. The music — 'Rock and Roll All Nite,' 'Love Gun,' and the Alive! spectacle of blood-spitting, fire-breathing personas — embodies Nietzsche's Dionysian, the raw instinctual side that Socratic rationalism suppressed, with concerts supplying the Dionysian fusion of the crowd. The band's transformations into the Demon and Starchild (which Gene and Paul describe as real, not acted), the face-painted audiences, and the taboo-breaking merchandise — KISS Kondoms that helped destigmatize condoms, the KISS Kasket that turned death into celebration as at Dimebag Darrell Abbott's funeral — enact Bakhtin's carnival, whose 'joyful relativity' decrowns the serious, with Zarathustra's 'free death' framing the Kasket as festival rather than mourning.

chapters.file: ch26 - 15. The Rashomon Effect in KISS’s Autobiographies.md
chapters.relation: Michael Forest and Matthew Mitchell read the four original members' autobiographies as a Rashomon effect, focused on the conflicting accounts of recording Destroyer and of who really wrote 'Beth.' Bernard Lonergan's 'scotosis' — the intellectual blind spot that censors evidence against our preferred view — explains how each memoirist constructs memories protecting his self-image, while Sartre's bad faith from Being and Nothingness (distinguished from lying via the woman-on-a-date example) explains how they may have deceived themselves rather than lied. Comparing Gene's, Ace's, Peter's, Paul's, and Lydia Criss's five accounts, the chapter concludes that no one is a reliable narrator and no one a sheer fabricator — and that fans reading the memoirs must guard against their own blind spots and bad faith.

chapters.file: ch27 - 16. KISS Goes Disco and Boogies on Simmons’s Bad Faith.md
chapters.relation: Christopher Innes defends 'I Was Made for Lovin' You' and KISS's disco turn on Dynasty against Gene Simmons's own scorn. Insisting that KISS is essentially and only hard rock treats the band's facticity as an in-itself, like Sartre's waiter who becomes nothing but his role — the bad faith of Simmons and rockist fans alike — whereas human transcendence and nothingness mean the band can authentically choose disco, grunge, or anything new, as Donna Summer's 'I Feel Love,' Pink Floyd, and Queen exemplify. The twist: bad faith is also a comfort, and the chapter ends by conceding that Simmons's hard-rock constancy may itself be an authentic filling of his own nothingness — so who is to say he is wrong?

Courtland Lewis tests philosophical theories of forgiveness against KISS's feuds. Jeffrie Murphy's account (overcoming vindictive resentment on moral grounds) shows Ace has not forgiven Gene's fired-three-times claims; Charles Griswold's twelve-condition 'paradigmatic forgiveness' is likely too demanding for them; Margaret Holmgren's compassionate character-forgiveness fits Bruce Kulick's and Eric Singer's graceful exits; and Geoffrey Scarre's utilitarian reading makes forgiveness a calculation of benefits. Lewis then applies his own rights-based peace-ethics (eireneism) to a thought experiment in which Gene steals Ace's drugs to save his flourishing — no wrong done, so no forgiveness needed — and closes by likening Paul and Gene to a married couple whose ongoing obligations model forgiveness, endorsing Wolfendale's refusal to call anyone unforgiveable.

chapters.file: ch30 - 18. What Does It Mean if the Band Plays Forever.md
chapters.relation: Robert Grant Price treats KISS's repeated farewell tours — the 2000 Farewell Tour followed by twelve more tours, then the End of the Road Tour — as false endings that keep reshaping the band's story, running two counterfactuals: folding in 1982 would have made a tragedy of celebrity, quitting after the 2001 Farewell Tour a comedy of graceful closure, while the actual open-ended career risks farce. He then asks whether an aging rock star can be wise, contrasting Stoic virtue — Marcus Aurelius's Meditations on self-control and humility, the cardinal virtues of Prudence, Fortitude, Justice, and Temperance — with the hedonism and libertinism of rock's party ethos, from 'Uh! All Night' to Bernini's Ecstasy of St. Teresa. Knowing when to place an ending, he concludes, is ultimately the philosophical question of what one's life is for.

Courtland Lewis uses KISS's reviled concept album Music from 'The Elder' as a case study in aesthetics. He contrasts objective theories of beauty (Plato and the Golden Ratio, tested against the 4/4 stomp of 'Rock and Roll All Nite') with Hume's taste and Kant's immediacy thesis that beauty is judged without inference, adds the disinterestedness of aesthetic pleasure, and applies Noel Carroll's moderate actual intentionalism (with Jerrold Levinson on what a musical work is) to argue that fans and band co-create the album's meaning. Peter French's collective memory explains why 'The Elder sucks' hardened into fan identity after Casablanca reordered the track listing and wrecked the boy-hero story, and Schopenhauer's claim that music expresses the in-itself of the world redeems the fans who find the album beautiful.

holes.name: Anton LaVey
holes.what: Founder of LaVeyan Satanism and author of The Satanic Bible, which promotes self-indulgence, individual freedom, and life-affirmation rather than devil-worship.
holes.why: Chapter 12 argues KISS's values overlap with LaVey's actual Satanism while debunking the demonic stereotype attached to the band.

holes.name: The Ethics of Belief (Clifford's evidentialism)
holes.what: W.K. Clifford's principle that it is wrong to believe or act on insufficient evidence, illustrated by the negligent shipowner thought experiment.
holes.why: Chapter 13 stages KISS's counter-evidence gamble on the Alive! live album against Clifford's demand for sufficient evidence before acting.

holes.name: Collective Intentionality
holes.what: The idea that shared 'we-intentions' of individuals create social and institutional facts such as teams, money, and brands.
holes.why: Chapter 15 argues that what KISS does, and whether a franchise band of hired musicians would even count as KISS, rests on the collective intentions of members and fans.

holes.name: Nicholas Wolterstorff
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose account of love distinguishes love as activity, as attachment, and as attraction (and whose memoir calls lives 'shot through with love').
holes.why: Chapter 20 uses Wolterstorff's three categories as the framework for sorting nearly every KISS song into kinds of love.

holes.name: Aristippus of Cyrene
holes.what: Founder of the Cyrenaic school, holding immediate bodily pleasure to be the highest good, pursued with self-control and an alternation of work and play.
holes.why: Chapter 21 reads KISS's sex songs and work-hard/play-hard ethos as a direct application of Aristippus's hedonism, including his cautions against overindulgence.

holes.name: Obligations to Future Generations
holes.what: The question whether present people owe duties to preserve resources, places, culture, or experiences for people who do not yet exist.
holes.why: Chapter 23 builds and tests the Preservationist claim that the rights of future generations give Gene and Paul a duty to keep KISS performing.

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian thinker whose theory of carnival holds that masking, laughter, and festivity suspend official hierarchies in an atmosphere of 'joyful relativity' that decrowns the serious.
holes.why: Chapter 25 reads KISS concerts, make-up transformations, and merchandise like the KISS Kondom and KISS Kasket as Bakhtinian carnival that lifts taboos on sex and death.

holes.name: Bernard Lonergan
holes.what: Canadian philosopher whose Insight names 'scotosis,' the intellectual blind spot that censors evidence against our entrenched interpretations.
holes.why: Chapter 26 uses Lonergan's scotosis to explain why each band member's memoir about recording 'Beth' suppresses inconvenient perspectives, alongside Sartre's bad faith.
